text: Karl Wilhelm Rudolf von Bennigsen (10 July 1824, Lüneburg – 7 August 1902, Bennigsen near Springe) was a German politician from an old Hanoverian family. He was born in Lüneburg on 10 July 1824; his father, Karl von Bennigsen, was a general in the Hanoverian Army and held diplomatic positions. His nephew was the anthropologist Moritz von Leonhardi. After studying at the University of Göttingen, where he joined the Corps Hannovera, Bennigsen entered the Hanoverian civil service. In 1855, he was elected to the second chamber, but resigned due to the government’s refusal to grant him leave from his duties. He then became the recognized leader of the Liberal opposition to the reactionary government, distinct from Alexander Levin, Count of Bennigsen, a member of the same family and son of the Russian General Bennigsen, who served as Hanover’s minister-president between 1848 and 1850 and later as president of both chambers of the Estates Assembly. Bennigsen’s significance extended across Germany through his role as founder and president of the German National Association, established in response to the Austro-Sardinian War, which aimed to promote national unity and constitutional liberty. The association united moderate Liberals and became a major political force despite government suppression, especially by King George V of Hanover. He was also a founder of the Protestantenverein in 1863. In 1866, as leader of the liberal opposition in the second chamber, he attempted to keep Hanover neutral in the Austro-Prussian War, though unsuccessfully; his brother, a Prussian Army officer, was killed in Bohemia. In May 1866, he had a significant meeting with Bismarck, who sought his support for reforming the German Confederation. After the war, Bennigsen became a Prussian subject and took a seat in the diet and the Prussian House of Representatives. He advocated for maximum autonomy for Hanover and opposed the Guelph Party. Alongside Ludwig Windthorst and Johann von Miquel, he was one of three Hanoverians who led the province’s representatives in both the Prussian and North German parliaments. The Nationalverein was dissolved after its work was completed, but Bennigsen was central in founding the National Liberals, who supported Bismarck’s national policy while seeking constitutional development. For the next thirty years, he served as president of the party and was the most influential parliamentary leader, helping avoid open conflict between Bismarck and parliament. He introduced numerous constitutional amendments and, in 1870, undertook a mission to Southern Germany to strengthen the national party, and was consulted by Bismarck at Versailles. He secured the compromise on the military bill in 1874. In 1877, he was offered the position of vice-chancellor with a seat in the Prussian ministry, but declined due to disagreements with Bismarck or the king over his conditions. From then on, his relations with the government became less friendly, and in 1878 he led the rejection of the first Socialist Bill. In 1883, he resigned from parliament due to reactionary government measures that ended his cooperation with Bismarck, but returned in 1887 to support a coalition of national parties. One of Emperor Wilhelm II’s first actions was to appoint him upper president of the Province of Hanover. In 1897, he resigned this post and retired from public life, dying on 7 August 1902.
